Most Amazon toy listings do not get suspended for a bad product. They get suspended for a document that does not match the ASIN, a warning label in the wrong place, or a category restriction nobody checked before the container shipped.
This is a working checklist, in the order the work actually happens. It complements the document-level detail in what gets a CPC rejected — here the focus is everything around the certificate that a reviewer also checks.
Requirements change. Confirm the current rules with a CPSC-accepted lab and your Amazon account manager before committing to a print run.
Stage 1 — before you order 1. Confirm the category is open to you. Toys & Games is a gated category in many marketplaces. Check whether you need approval, and whether approval requires documents up front. Finding out after production is a five-figure mistake.
2. Check the product against recall history. Search the CPSC recall database and the EU Safety Gate for the product type. Fidgets, magnetic building sets, water beads and button-cell novelties have long recall histories. If your item resembles a recalled product, expect scrutiny.
3. Confirm restricted sub-categories. High-powered magnets are regulated in the US; water beads and some projectile toys face marketplace restrictions; laser toys, chemistry sets and toy guns have their own rules. Amazon applies its own policy on top of the law, and it is stricter than the law.
4. Fix the age grade before tooling. The age grade drives the test protocol, the warning text, the small-parts assessment and the listing attributes. An age grade changed after testing means retesting.
5. Fix the importer identity. In the US, the CPC must name the importer of record. In the EU, the listing and label must name the EU responsible person. Decide these parties before the labels are printed — both appear on packaging.
Stage 2 — testing and documents 6. US: CPC built from a CPSC-accepted lab report. The lab report is not the certificate; the importer issues the CPC. It must reference the model/ASIN, the age grade, the rules tested (ASTM F963 and CPSIA at minimum), and the lab’s acceptance number. See the CPC guide for the five rejection reasons.
7. US: CPSIA tracking label. Children’s products need a permanent mark on the product and its packaging showing manufacturer or private labeler name, location and date of production, and a batch or cohort identifier. A carton barcode alone is not a tracking label. This is one of the most common review failures because factories often print it as an afterthought, or not at all.
8. EU: CE marking, DoC and test reports. EN 71-1/2/3 for the toy, plus EN 62115 for anything electrical, plus EMC or radio approval where applicable. The Declaration of Conformity must name the product and the standards applied.
9. EU: GPSR listing fields. Since 13 December 2024 the marketplace listing must show the manufacturer’s name and address, the EU responsible person’s name, postal address and email, and product safety information. Amazon enforces this in the listing back end. The full requirement set is in the GPSR guide.
10. Battery documents, if the toy contains a battery. UN38.3 report, MSDS and test summary for the cell or pack, plus the applicable FCC or RED approval for anything that transmits. Amazon asks for these for FBA inbound lithium shipments. Details are in the RC and electronic toy guide.
11. Photograph the actual label. Reviewers want to see the warning text, the tracking label or CE mark, the importer address and the age grade as printed on the retail unit. A mock-up from the design file is not proof that production matches.
Stage 3 — the warning text Warning wording is where small errors cost the most, because it is printed.
Situation Required wording (US) Note Small parts, under 3 “WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD — Small parts. Not for children under 3 yrs.” Exact wording and layout; do not paraphrase Small ball “WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD — This toy is a small ball. Not for children under 3 yrs.” Ball-specific variant Balloon “WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD — Children under 8 yrs. can choke or suffocate on uninflated or broken balloons.” Age 8, not 3 Battery toy Battery safety and disposal statement Plus compartment tool requirement where applicable Button/coin cell Prescribed ingestion warning Required on product and packaging In the EU, warnings must be in the language of the country of sale, and the CE mark plus age warning must be on the product or packaging. Do not put the EU responsible person’s details only in the listing — GPSR requires them on the product or packaging too.
Check the print size against the standard before the plates are made. A warning printed at 4 pt on a dark background fails review even when the words are right.
Stage 4 — listing build 12. Main image on pure white, product only. No props, no logos, no text overlays. Toys attract lifestyle imagery, but the main image slot is not the place for it.
13. Every accessory in the box is photographed. “Set” listings with undisclosed pieces generate returns and authenticity complaints. If the box contains a charger, a strap or a spare wheel, show it.
14. Attributes match the certificate. Age range, material, battery type, number of pieces, and the model number must mirror the CPC or DoC. A mismatch between the listing and the document is treated as a compliance failure, not a data-entry error.
15. Restricted-claims check. Avoid “non-toxic”, “100% safe”, “FDA approved” and similar unless literally true and documented. Toy listings that claim absolute safety attract both complaints and regulatory attention.
16. Packaging suffocation warning. Polybags need the suffocation warning, and a bag above the size threshold needs the warning plus a hole or a thickness spec. Amazon’s FBA prep rules also require it. See packaging cost comparison for how the bag type interacts with cost.
17. FBA prep for sets and multipacks. “Sold as a set of 3” on the outer polybag, no combined barcodes, and each unit correctly labelled if it can be sold separately.
Stage 5 — when Amazon asks for documents A compliance review usually arrives as a case in the product compliance area of Seller Central, with a deadline. What clears it fastest:
A single PDF per document, clearly named by ASIN and document type. The CPC or DoC on letterhead, signed, dated, with the importer’s name and address. The full lab report behind it, not just the summary page. Product images showing the label and the packaged unit. If the document is older than a material change, say so and supply the new one — do not submit a report that silently predates a supplier change. What reliably fails: a certificate for a different model, a report from a lab without CPSC acceptance, a document with the factory as importer when you are the importer, and a photo of a label that does not match the listing’s age grade.
Restricted and high-scrutiny items Some toy types deserve a decision before sourcing rather than after:
Item Status to verify High-powered magnet sets Regulated in the US; strict marketplace restrictions Water beads Marketplace restrictions; ingestion hazard Button-cell novelties Child-resistant compartment and warnings required Laser toys Classification and label rules; some classes not sellable Projectile toys Energy limits and tip requirements Chemistry sets Age grading and hazard labelling Toy guns / realistic replicas Marketplace policy restrictions in many countries If a supplier offers a “hot” item with no documentation, that is the item most likely to be pulled from the catalogue three months later, taking your inventory with it.
The one-page pre-launch checklist Category gated? Approval obtained or plan confirmed Product checked against CPSC and Safety Gate recalls Age grade fixed and consistent across test, label and listing Importer (US) and responsible person (EU) identified and printed CPC issued by the importer, referencing the model and lab acceptance number CPSIA tracking label on product and packaging EN 71 + EN 62115 + EMC/radio reports for the EU GPSR listing fields complete UN38.3 + MSDS + test summary if a battery is included Warning text exact, in the right language, at the right size Label photographed from a production unit Main image white background, product only All box contents photographed Attributes match the certificate Polybag suffocation warning and FBA set labelling Documents renamed and archived by ASIN Restricted-item review completed The short version The certificate is one item on a checklist, not the checklist. Tracking labels, warning wording, age grading and importer identity cause as many failures as the test report. The EU now enforces listing-level manufacturer and responsible-person fields; the US enforces tracking labels. Battery toys need transport documents as well as safety reports. Decide age grade, importer and responsible person before anything is printed. Our quality and compliance page lists the document set we coordinate per market, and the toy catalogue shows the categories we produce with testing already mapped. If you are preparing a launch, send the ASIN plan and target marketplace and we will return the required document list and the label fields before you place the order.
For the underlying test logic by market, see EN71, ASTM F963 and GPSR.

Since 13 December 2024, every toy placed on the EU market is covered by the General Product Safety Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/988 — usually shortened to GPSR. It replaced the 2001 General Product Safety Directive, and it changed something that catches Chinese suppliers and their customers repeatedly: the party liable for a product’s safety must be established inside the EU, and that fact must appear on the product, the packaging and the online listing.
CE marking and an EN71 test report do not satisfy GPSR. They are separate obligations that now stack.
What GPSR is, and what it is not GPSR Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC Scope All consumer products Toys specifically Core concern General safety, traceability, responsibility Toy-specific safety, EN71 tests Key output Risk assessment, technical file, responsible person Test reports, CE marking, DoC Status Applies from 13 Dec 2024 Still in force; replacement regulation in the legislative pipeline A toy sold in the EU needs both. GPSR does not replace the toy-specific requirements; it adds a layer of traceability and accountability on top of them. For the toy-specific side, see EN71, ASTM and GPSR compared.
The six obligations that matter to a seller 1. Only safe products may be placed on the market. This sounds obvious, but GPSR requires you to be able to demonstrate safety through a documented risk assessment — not just a test report. The assessment must consider foreseeable use, including by children and vulnerable users.
2. An EU-established responsible person (RP). A manufacturer outside the EU must designate a natural or legal person established in the EU. Their name, postal address and email must appear on the product or its packaging, and in the online listing. The RP must be able to produce the technical file on request and cooperate with market surveillance authorities.
3. Traceability. The product must carry identification that lets authorities trace the batch or serial number, plus the manufacturer’s name and address. A generic “Made in China” is not sufficient.
4. Technical documentation, kept for 10 years. Includes the risk assessment, test reports, declarations of conformity, and manufacturing records.
5. Online listing disclosures. This is where most Amazon and Shopify sellers get caught. See the table below.
6. Incident reporting and corrective action. Serious incidents and recalls must be notified through the EU Safety Business Gateway. If a product is unsafe, you must withdraw or recall it.
What your listing must show GPSR’s online sales provisions require the following to be visible before purchase:
Required on the listing Detail Manufacturer name Legal entity name Manufacturer postal address Full address, not a city only Manufacturer email A working contact RP name and address If the manufacturer is outside the EU RP email A working contact Product identification Type, batch or serial number Product images Clear, showing the product as sold Warnings and safety info In the language of the member state of sale Amazon has been enforcing this through its compliance portal: sellers are asked to upload RP details and may be blocked from listing without them. Marketplaces are treated as having their own obligations under GPSR, which is why they push the requirement onto sellers aggressively.
Who can be the responsible person The RP must be a physical or legal person established in the EU. Realistic options:
Option Suitable when Typical cost Your EU importer You sell via a distributor who imports Included in the relationship An authorised representative service You sell direct / via marketplace EUR 200–600 per year, sometimes per SKU An EU fulfilment service provider You use an EU 3PL and they agree Often bundled, but confirm in writing Your own EU entity You have or open an EU company Company costs A Chinese factory or a Chinese sourcing agent cannot act as RP. If a supplier tells you they will be your responsible person, they are either misunderstanding the regulation or describing an arrangement that will not survive an authority’s check. Our quality and compliance service prepares the technical file and the label artwork, but the RP appointment itself must be made by an EU-established entity.
The five misunderstandings we see most “We have CE and EN71, so we are covered.” CE marking plus test reports cover the toy-specific safety requirements. GPSR adds traceability, an RP and listing disclosures on top. Both are needed.
“Our freight forwarder will be the responsible person.” A forwarder moving goods through customs is not automatically an RP. They may offer the service, but it must be a written appointment with the obligations spelled out.
“GPSR only affects large sellers.” It applies to every product placed on the EU market, including a 50-piece test order sold on Etsy.
“The importer of record handles it.” If you sell direct to consumers from China via a marketplace, you may be the one placing the product on the market, and the obligation is yours. This is precisely the situation GPSR was designed to close.
“A label with our company name is enough.” The label must carry the manufacturer’s details and the RP’s details, plus batch identification. A brand logo is neither.
A practical compliance checklist For each toy SKU you sell into the EU:
[ ] Risk assessment document (foreseeable use, age group, hazards) [ ] EN71-1/-2/-3 test reports from an accredited lab, current batch [ ] EU Declaration of Conformity, signed [ ] Technical file assembled, stored 10 years [ ] Responsible person appointed, written agreement in place [ ] Product label: manufacturer name, address, email, batch ID [ ] Product label: RP name, address, email [ ] Packaging warnings in the language of the sale country [ ] Listing updated with all fields in the table above [ ] Incident reporting process defined (Safety Business Gateway) If several of these are missing on a product you already sell, the exposure is not theoretical. Market surveillance authorities can order a withdrawal, and non-compliance penalties vary by member state — some run into the millions of euros for repeated or serious breaches. Marketplaces, meanwhile, simply delist.
Where this fits in the buying process The practical sequence for a new toy order into the EU:
Before tooling: confirm the age grade and decide who will be the RP. Sample stage: commission EN71 testing on the final materials and artwork. Before mass production: complete the risk assessment and the DoC. Before shipping: finalise the label artwork — it is printed, so mistakes are expensive. Before listing: fill in every GPSR field on the marketplace. Label artwork is the step where we see the most avoidable cost. Printing 5,000 cartons without the RP’s address means either reprinting or stickering every unit. Review the label against the checklist before the plates are made — see packaging costs for how late artwork changes affect the whole order.
The short version GPSR has applied since 13 December 2024 and covers all toys sold in the EU. You need an EU-established responsible person, and their details must be on the product, packaging and listing. CE and EN71 are still required and are not a substitute. Technical files must be kept for 10 years. Marketplaces are enforcing this now, not eventually. If you are planning an EU launch and want the document set and label layout prepared in one pass, our compliance page lists what we supply per market and the turnaround. The one thing we cannot do for you is be your responsible person — that requires an EU entity, and we will tell you the same thing any honest supplier should.

Japan and Korea are the two Asian markets most buyers underestimate. Both have mature toy regulations, both test for the same hazards as the EU and US, and neither will accept an EN71 report or a CPC as evidence.
The practical difference is who carries the paperwork. In the EU you appoint a responsible person; in Japan and Korea the importer is the accountable party, and in Korea the certificate must be held by a Korean-registered business. That single fact determines how you structure the shipment.
Japan: the ST Mark What it is The ST Mark (STマーク) is the toy safety mark administered by the Japan Toy Association (JTA). It is voluntary under law but effectively mandatory in commerce: major retailers, e-commerce platforms and distributors expect it, and a toy without it is difficult to place in any serious channel.
The ST Standard is published in three parts:
Part Covers Part 1 Physical and mechanical properties — sharp edges, small parts, cords, entrapment Part 2 Flammability — burn rate for soft and plush toys, surface flash Part 3 Chemical properties — heavy metals, phthalates, formaldehyde, dye migration Age divisions follow the same logic as EN 71: under 36 months, 3–6, 6–14 and 14+. The age symbol printed with the mark tells the consumer which group the toy was assessed for, and it has to match the toy’s actual design and warnings.
The legal layer underneath The ST Mark is not the only requirement. Three laws can apply on top of it:
Consumer Product Safety Act (CPSA). Certain categories require the PSC mark and a business notification to METI. Some infant and toddler toys and magnet-based play products fall into this group. Food Sanitation Act. Toys that infants may put in their mouths — teethers, rattles, some soft toys — are regulated for material safety, and imports are notified at the quarantine station. PSE and the Radio Act. Battery toys are outside PSE, but any mains adapter needs PSE. Bluetooth or radio-controlled toys need the technical conformity mark (技適). A toy can therefore need the ST Mark plus one or more of these, and each has its own testing and labelling.
Who applies, and how long it takes The ST Mark is licensed through the Japan Toy Association, and testing is done by designated institutes. Your Japanese importer or distributor is normally the licence holder; a Chinese factory cannot hold it on your behalf.
Budget roughly 3–5 weeks for testing plus admin for one model family, with costs in the low thousands of US dollars per family depending on the number of parts and colours tested. A “model family” — same construction, same materials, different colours or sizes — reduces cost substantially compared with testing each SKU separately, so group your range deliberately before you send samples.
Label requirements in practice Japanese retailers will reject a carton for label issues faster than for almost anything else. The sewn-in or applied label should carry:
ST Mark with the correct age symbol Manufacturer or importer name and address (in Japanese) Country of origin Target age and the required warnings in Japanese Batch or lot identification The Japanese warning text is conventional and short — “対象年齢” plus the specific hazard statement — but it must be present and legible at retail size. Approve the label artwork with your importer before printing.
Korea: KC confirmation for children’s products What it is Korea regulates toys under the Special Act on Safety Management of Children’s Products. Toys are “children’s products”, and most toys sit in the safety confirmation (안전확인) route: a sample is tested by an accredited laboratory, a report is issued, and the product is registered with the KC mark and a confirmation number.
The KC mark is not optional. Without it the product cannot be customs-cleared for sale or listed on Korean platforms.
What gets tested Korean toy testing overlaps heavily with EN 71 but is not identical:
Physical and mechanical hazards, including small parts for under-36-month toys Flammability Heavy metal migration and phthalates Labelling and warnings in Korean Because the standards are national, an existing EN71 or ASTM report shortens the work — your lab can reuse data — but it does not replace the Korean report.
Who can apply This is the constraint that catches first-time sellers. The certificate holder must be a Korean-registered business. A Chinese manufacturer or a foreign brand cannot hold it directly. In practice you have three options:
Sell to a Korean importer who holds the confirmation and re-labels under their own name. Appoint a Korean distributor as the applicant, with a written agreement about who owns the mark and the test data. Use a Korean compliance agency that acts as the applicant and importer of record, which is workable but adds a party to the supply chain. Decide this before you quote, because it changes the Incoterms and the price. Selling DDP to a Korean warehouse is not the same as selling to an importer who will hold the KC.
Label requirements Korean labels are strict and specific. Expect to show:
KC mark and the safety confirmation number Product name and model Manufacturer name and address, plus the importer’s name and address Country of origin Manufacturing date (제조년월) — a month and year, not just a year Age range and warnings in Korean Weight or quantity where applicable The manufacturing date is the field most often missing from Chinese factory labels, because it is not a common requirement elsewhere. Add it to the label artwork from the first draft.
Japan vs Korea vs EU vs US at a glance Japan ST Korea KC EU CE / EN71 US CPC Legal status Voluntary, commercially required Mandatory Mandatory Mandatory Who holds it Japanese importer / JTA licence Korean-registered business EU manufacturer or RP US importer / brand Core tests Mechanical, flammability, chemical Mechanical, flammability, chemical EN 71-1/2/3 ASTM F963 + CPSIA Local-language label Japanese Korean Sale-country language English Report transferable No No No No The pattern is consistent: each market wants its own report, its own mark and a label in its own language, held by a party established in that market.
Planning the sequence For a toy going to both countries, the order that avoids rework:
Lock the design and materials first. Every change after testing means a new report. Send samples to both labs at the same time. The tests overlap; the reports do not. Confirm the applicant in each market — importer in Japan, Korean business in Korea — before testing starts, because the certificate is issued to them. Draft both labels in parallel. The Korean label needs the manufacturing month; the Japanese label needs the age symbol. Both need the importer’s address, which you only know once step 3 is settled. Test, then print. Never print labels on the assumption that testing will pass. Plastic parts and printed inks are the usual failures, and they are fixable — after the report, not before. Ship. Keep the report numbers, the confirmation number and the label artwork in the technical file alongside your EN71 or CPC documents. The mistakes that cost the most Assuming an EN71 report will be accepted. It will not, in either market. It may reduce the test scope, nothing more. Testing one colour of a multi-colour range. Korean and Japanese labs commonly require each colourway, because pigments and plasticisers differ. Group SKUs by material, not by artwork. Forgetting the importer on the label. A label with only the Chinese factory address fails in both countries. Printing labels before the test report. A failed phthalate test on a printed part means reprinting every carton. Treating ST as optional because it is voluntary. Retailers enforce it; a toy without the mark simply does not get shelf space. The short version Japan: ST Mark from the Japan Toy Association — voluntary in law, required in practice, licensed through your Japanese importer. Korea: KC safety confirmation under the children’s products act — mandatory, and the certificate must be held by a Korean-registered business. Neither market accepts an EN71 report or a CPC; both need local testing and local-language labels. Korea requires the manufacturing month on the label; Japan requires the ST age symbol. Settle the applicant and the label artwork before testing, and group your SKUs by material to control cost. Our compliance page lists the reports we coordinate per market, including ST and KC through partner labs, and the RC and electronic toy category covers the PSE and radio-mark questions that come with battery toys. If you are planning a Japan or Korea launch, send the SKU list and target retail price and we will map the testing scope and the label fields before you commit to tooling.
For the EU and US side of the same comparison, see EN71, ASTM F963 and GPSR and the CPC guide for Amazon sellers.

Japan and Korea are the two Asian markets most buyers underestimate. Both have mature toy regulations, both test for the same hazards as the EU and US, and neither will accept an EN71 report or a CPC as evidence.

The practical difference is who carries the paperwork. In the EU you appoint a responsible person; in Japan and Korea the importer is the accountable party, and in Korea the certificate must be held by a Korean-registered business. That single fact determines how you structure the shipment.

content:
Almost every toy order from China runs on a deposit. The interesting question is not whether you pay 30% up front — it is what happens to the other 70%, who verifies the goods, and what the factory can do if you refuse to pay.
Payment terms are where trust is either built slowly or lost in a single transaction. Here is how the standard structures actually work, and the specific patterns that mean you should stop.
The five structures you will be offered Structure Typical use Risk sits with 30% deposit / 70% before shipment Standard for most toy orders Buyer (until goods ship) 30% deposit / 70% after inspection Preferred by experienced buyers Shared 100% T/T in advance Small orders, first-time, low value Buyer entirely L/C at sight Orders above USD 50,000–100,000 Bank-mediated Trade Assurance / escrow Alibaba and similar platforms Platform (partially) 30/70 before shipment is the default because it protects the factory’s cash flow: materials must be bought before production. The buyer’s protection comes from inspection before the balance is paid — which only works if you actually inspect, or appoint someone who does.
30/70 after inspection is the structure to ask for on any order above roughly USD 3,000. It reads: deposit on PO, balance released after the pre-shipment inspection report is accepted. Most factories accept this; a factory that refuses it on a first order is telling you something.
100% in advance is normal for stock items under a few hundred dollars and for sample orders. Above that, it is a red flag unless you have a long relationship.
L/C at sight costs 0.5–1.5% in bank fees and requires precise documentation — one typo can delay payment by weeks. It is worth it for large orders with a new factory, and unnecessary for small ones.
Trade Assurance gives you a platform-mediated dispute process. It is genuinely useful for a first order, but the coverage is limited to the terms recorded in the order, so the specification must be written into the order itself, not agreed by chat.
What the deposit actually covers The 30% is not a security deposit. It is working capital for:
Fabric and trims purchased up front Mould or plate costs, if any Labour scheduled on a production line Packaging printed before assembly If you cancel after the deposit is paid, the factory has already spent part of it. This is why deposits are usually non-refundable, and why the contract should say what happens to unused materials if an order is cancelled mid-production.
The clause that matters more than the percentage The payment split protects nobody if the specification is vague. Put the acceptance criteria in the PO:
1. Deposit: 30% on PO signature, T/T. 2. Balance: 70% within 5 working days after buyer accepts the pre-shipment inspection report (AQL II, major 2.5 / minor 4.0). 3. Inspection: third-party or buyer-appointed, at factory, 7 days before scheduled shipment. 4. If inspection fails: factory reworks and re-inspects at its own cost. Buyer may cancel if a second inspection fails, with deposit refunded less material actually consumed. 5. Late delivery: 0.5% of order value per week, capped at 5%. 6. Golden sample signed by both parties is the quality reference. Item 2 is the one that changes behaviour. When the balance depends on an inspection result, the factory manages quality upstream instead of hoping.
Bank fraud: the risk nobody warns you about Business email compromise is common in Chinese sourcing, and it targets exactly this moment: the week before you send the 70%.
The pattern:
You agree terms with a real factory, using a real email address. Weeks later, an email arrives from a near-identical address — one character different, or the display name matches but the domain is factory-co.com instead of factory.com — saying the company has changed banks and the balance should go to a new account. The account is real, in Hong Kong or Shenzhen, and the money is gone. The defence is mechanical, not clever:
Verify any bank change by phone, calling a number you already had — never a number in the email. Compare the account name to the company name on the contract. A mismatch (paying a personal name or a third-party trading company) requires an explanation in writing. Never accept a bank change sent only by email, even from a correct address. Treat it as fraud until confirmed by voice. Pay the deposit and balance to the same account unless there is a documented reason. We have seen buyers lose a full 70% balance this way. It is the single most expensive mistake in the whole sourcing process, and it is entirely preventable with one phone call.
Red flags that mean stop Signal Why it matters Insists on 100% advance on a first order above USD 3,000 Transfers all risk to you Requests payment to a personal account No legal recourse, likely tax/export irregularity Changes bank details by email only Classic BEC fraud pattern Refuses third-party inspection Has something to hide, or cannot meet spec No business licence or export rights Cannot legally export; goods may be seized Price far below market with no explanation Material substitution is coming Asks for payment in crypto No traceability, no dispute process The last two are also a signal about how the rest of the relationship will go. A factory that cuts corners on payment paperwork cuts corners on fabric weight.
When to walk away Walk away — not negotiate — when:
A bank change cannot be confirmed by phone with a number you already had. No exceptions. The company name on the invoice does not match the payee, and the explanation is verbal only. They refuse inspection but want the balance before loading. You are being asked to pay blind. They demand 100% advance on a first order over USD 3,000 and will not accept 30/70 with inspection. In each case, there are hundreds of other factories. The cost of finding another supplier is a week. The cost of a bad payment is the entire order.
A workable default For a first order with a new factory:
30% deposit on PO 70% after third-party AQL inspection, before shipment Third-party inspection cost: USD 250–350/day (Zhejiang) Payment to the company named on the contract, verified by phone Golden sample signed and retained by both parties Late-delivery penalty in the PO This structure is standard enough that reputable factories accept it without argument, and strict enough that the ones who refuse are telling you what you need to know. Our how to order page documents the version we use on every order, including what happens if inspection fails twice.
For the cost side of the same decision — how payment timing affects your cash cycle — see landed cost.

content:
Plush is the category where quotes diverge the most — three suppliers, three prices, sometimes a 3x spread. The reason is rarely the factory’s margin. It is that “a 25 cm teddy bear in soft fabric” describes a product with perhaps forty undefined variables, and every factory fills the gaps differently.
This guide covers the three that move cost and safety most: fabric, filling and construction. It ends with the inspection checks that tell you whether you received what you specified.
Fabric: the four numbers that define it Ask for these explicitly. A supplier who cannot answer them is quoting from a catalogue, not from a specification.
Parameter Typical range Why it matters Fibre content 100% polyester (most common); acrylic; cotton blends Determines feel, pilling, dye behaviour and price Weight 180–450 g/m² The single biggest cost driver after size; 220 vs 380 g/m² is a different product Pile height 1–20 mm (velboa 2–3 mm, long-pile 10–20 mm) Visual “plushness”; long pile sheds and traps dust Backing Knitted or woven backing, with or without backing glue Thin backing tears at seams; glue can fail at low temperature Two fabrics can look identical in a photo and differ by 40% in cost. Velboa at 250 g/m² is the workhorse for toys under about 25 cm. Long-pile “fur” at 500 g/m² and above is what makes a large bear feel expensive — and it is also the fabric that fails fire testing most often.
Ask for a fabric swatch with the weight written on the label, and keep it. When the bulk arrives, a GSM cutter (a circular punch and a scale) settles any dispute in two minutes.
Dyed-lot and colour matching Fabric is dyed in batches. If your order runs across two dye lots, the light pink of carton one and carton two may not match — and on a retail shelf that reads as a quality problem. For orders above roughly 2,000 pcs in one colour, specify “single dye lot” in the PO. Expect a surcharge if the mill has to hold the lot.
For a licensed or Pantone-matched colour, provide the Pantone reference and require a lab-dip approval before bulk fabric is cut. Approving colour from a phone photo is how returns happen.
Filling: what is actually inside Almost all plush filling is polyester fibre — “PP cotton” in factory language. The variables are grade and weight.
Filling Character Where it is used Hollow conjugated siliconised fibre Springs back, stays lofty after washing Standard for quality plush Solid fibre Cheaper, packs down, lumps after washing Low-cost promotional plush Recycled PET fibre (rPET) Same performance if specified correctly; needs certification EU and US buyers with sustainability claims Micro-bead / EPS pellets Weighted feel (bean bags, “weighted” plush) Niche; adds small-parts and labelling obligations Specify fill weight in grams per unit, not “stuffed firmly”. A 30 cm bear typically takes 120–180 g; the same bear at 80 g feels hollow within a week. Ask the factory to weigh the first article on a scale and record it — that number goes into the inspection checklist.
Two failure modes are common and both are invisible until the customer opens the box:
Offcut filling. Some low-cost factories stuff with fabric offcuts or non-woven waste. It smells, it clumps, and it can contain loose fibres that fail small-parts assessment. Require “100% polyester fibre filling, no offcuts” in writing. Under-filling to hit a price. A quote that is 15% below the others is often 30% less filling. Since filling is cheap relative to fabric, this is a poor trade — but it is the easiest one for a factory to make silently. If you make an rPET or recycled-content claim, the fibre supplier’s certification (GRS or equivalent) must be in the technical file. A claim without a certificate is a compliance risk, not a marketing asset.
Construction: where safety lives Eyes, noses and attached parts This is the detail that decides whether a toy can be sold to children under three.
Option Safety profile Cost Embroidered eyes and nose No detachable part; safest for 0–3 Higher labour, lower material Safety eyes with washer lock Passes tension testing when correctly set Low Glued or screw-on eyes Should not be used on children’s plush Low, and not worth the risk Plastic nose with prongs Acceptable if it passes pull testing Low EN 71-1 applies a 90 N tension and 0.34 N·m torque test to components that a child could grip; ASTM F963 uses comparable pull and torque tests. Whether a safety eye passes depends less on the eye than on the washer being properly seated and the fabric not tearing around it. That is a factory skill, and it is why plush from an unverified workshop is a gamble even when the components are correct.
For anything labelled 0–3, embroidered features remove the question entirely. We default to embroidery on infant plush for that reason.
Seams and stitching Seam type: overlock or flatlock for the body, back-stitch at stress points (arm and leg joins, neck). Stitch density: 8–12 stitches per inch. Too loose and the filling escapes; too tight and the fabric puckers. Seam strength: the seam should not open under a firm manual pull at the arm and leg joins. Ask for the first article to be pull-tested and photographed. Closing seam: the final closure (usually the bottom) is the weakest point. It must be hand-stitched with a locked finish, not spot-glued. Embellishments Appliqué, heat-transfer print and embroidery all add cost and all add failure points. Heat-transfer prints crack after washing; specify wash testing at 40 °C if the toy is machine washable. Sequins, ribbons and bows on infant toys are a small-parts risk and should be avoided below three years.
Fire safety: EN 71-2 and ASTM F963 Plush is a soft toy, and soft toys are tested for flammability in both major markets.
EN 71-2 assesses the rate at which flame spreads across the surface. Soft toys must not exceed the standard’s maximum burn rate — in the current version, 30 mm/s — and surface flash is also assessed. Long-pile and brushed fabrics are the ones that fail; dense velboa at 250–300 g/m² generally passes without treatment.
ASTM F963 Section 4.2 sets a burn-rate limit for soft toys in the US market. In practice most polyester plush passes, but acrylic pile and very open, fluffy constructions are the risk cases.
Two practical points:
Test the actual fabric, not a similar one. A supplier who says “our fabric already passed EN71-2” is telling you about a different roll. The test report must reference the fabric weight and composition you are buying. Do not accept a flame retardant as the fix without asking what it is. Some FR chemistries are restricted under REACH or create their own compliance problem. Changing the fabric is usually cleaner than treating it. Always confirm current test parameters with your lab before you commit to a report — standards are amended, and the version matters for a CPC or DoC.
Chemical and labelling obligations Plush is mouthable by design, which brings the chemical tests into scope:
EN 71-3 — migration of heavy metals from the fabric, prints and plastic parts. REACH Annex XVII — azo dyes, formaldehyde, and restricted substances in the textile. CPSIA — total lead limit (100 ppm in substrate), phthalates at 0.1% in plasticised parts, plus a CPC for US import. Age grading and warnings — the CE mark, the age symbol (0–3 or 3+), and the “not suitable for children under 36 months” warning where applicable, in the language of the sale country. Label artwork is printed on the sewn-in label and often on the hangtag, so mistakes are expensive to correct. Approve the artwork before the labels are produced, not after.
The five inspection checks that catch bad plush At AQL Level II pre-shipment, add these five to the standard checklist:
Fabric weight. Cut a 100 cm² sample from a random unit, weigh it, compare to the approved swatch. Below 90% of spec is a fail. Fill weight. Weigh three units per size and compare to the first-article record. Pull test. Apply a firm manual pull to eyes, noses and the closing seam on a sample of units. Needle and metal detection. Every plush line should pass through a metal detector, with a documented broken-needle policy. This is standard for plush and is skipped by small workshops. Wash test. Wash one unit at the labelled temperature and check for colour bleeding, pilling, filling clumping and print cracking. The rest is standard: label text, barcode scan, carton drop, packing count, and visual defects against the approved sample.
How to write the spec so quotes are comparable A plush spec sheet that factories can quote from without guessing:
Item: Teddy bear, sitting, 28 cm Fabric: 100% polyester velboa, 280 g/m², colour Pantone 7529 C, head pile 3 mm Filling: 100% polyester hollow siliconised fibre, 150 g per unit, no offcuts Features: embroidered eyes and nose; embroidery on chest 4,000 stitches Seams: overlock body, back-stitch at limb joins, hand-stitched locked closure Age grade: 0+ (EN 71-1/2/3 and CPSIA testing required) Label: sewn-in care label + hangtag, artwork approved before production Packaging: 1 pc per polybag with suffocation warning, 40 pcs per export carton Testing: EN 71-1/2/3 report for this fabric weight and colour Target price: FOB Ningbo, 1,000 / 3,000 / 5,000 pcs Send the same sheet to every supplier. The quotes you get back will then differ for real reasons — factory size, labour, fabric buying power — rather than for undefined specification. For why the spread still exists and how to read it, see why custom plush quotes differ by 3x.
The short version Fabric weight in g/m² and pile height decide both cost and fire performance; put them in the PO. Specify filling grade and grams per unit — under-filling is the most common silent cost cut. Embroidered features are the safest choice for under-three plush; safety eyes depend on how the washer is set. EN 71-2 and ASTM F963 test the actual fabric, not a generic “plush” claim. Add fabric weight, fill weight, pull test, needle detection and a wash test to every plush inspection. If you are developing a plush line, our plush toy category shows the constructions we produce most often, and the quality and compliance page lists the reports supplied per market. Send a sketch or a reference photo and we will come back with a spec sheet and a comparable quote.
summary:
Plush is the category where quotes diverge the most — three suppliers, three prices, sometimes a 3x spread. The reason is rarely the factory’s margin. It is that “a 25 cm teddy bear in soft fabric” describes a product with perhaps forty undefined variables, and every factory fills the gaps differently.

This guide covers the three that move cost and safety most: fabric, filling and construction. It ends with the inspection checks that tell you whether you received what you specified.

A plush toy and an RC car can share the same fabric, the same carton and the same buyer — and still be completely different compliance problems. The moment a toy contains a battery, three new systems switch on: electrical safety, radio regulation and dangerous-goods freight.
Most of the avoidable cost in this category comes from one decision made too late: whether the battery ships inside the toy. That decision changes the unit cost, the test scope, the freight rate and the returns rate. Make it before you quote, not after.
Decision one: is the battery included? Battery included Battery excluded Unit cost Higher; factory sources and installs cells Lower; buyer sources locally Compliance Full electrical + transport scope Electrical scope only, no UN38.3 shipment Freight Lithium dangerous goods rules apply Ordinary cargo in most cases Retail readiness Sells straight off the shelf Buyer or retailer must add batteries Returns risk Battery faults become your fault Battery faults become the customer’s For Amazon and retail channels, “batteries included” sells better and is often required for gift sets. For promotional and B2B orders, “batteries not included” is normal and cheaper. Do not let a factory default this for you — state it in the PO, because a last-minute change invalidates the test report and the label.
Battery chemistry: what to specify Chemistry Typical use What to watch AA / AAA alkaline Budget RC, light-up toys Leakage in storage; specify brand-grade cells, not unbranded Li-ion 18650 / 14500 Rechargeable RC cars, drones Capacity fraud is common; require cell datasheet + IEC 62133 report LiPo pouch Slim drones, thin remote controls Swelling; needs a protection circuit board (PCB) NiMH Rechargeable, replaceable Self-discharge; lower voltage per cell Coin / button cell Sound modules, LED novelties Child-resistance rules; the highest-risk component in the toy The most expensive mistake in this table is the 18650. Cells advertised at 3,000 mAh that deliver 900 mAh are common in low-cost Yiwu supply, and the failure shows up as a 20-minute run time and a one-star review. Ask for the cell datasheet, the IEC 62133 report for the cell, and a capacity test on production samples.
What the standards actually cover Electrical toys are not just “toys with a battery”. Four separate scopes stack:
Scope EU US Japan Korea Toy safety EN 71-1/2/3 ASTM F963 + CPSIA ST Standard KC safety confirmation Electrical toy safety EN 62115 ASTM F963 §4.25 (battery toys) ST Part 1 + electrical clauses KC electrical clauses EMC EMC Directive 2014/30/EU FCC Part 15 (unintentional) — KC EMC Radio Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU FCC Part 15 (intentional, FCC ID) Radio Act (技適) KC (Radio Waves Act) A 2.4 GHz RC car therefore needs toy testing, electrical testing, EMC and radio approval in each market — four reports, not one. An EN 62115 report does not satisfy the FCC, and an FCC grant does not satisfy the RED.
EN 62115 is the electric toy standard, and it tests things a general toy report does not: heating under normal and abnormal operation, motor stall, mechanical strength of the enclosure, battery compartment construction, protection against access to live parts, and the charger input. If your factory’s report says “EN 71 tested” and nothing else, the electrical scope is missing.
Radio: the part buyers forget Any toy that transmits — RC cars, drones, Bluetooth speakers, app-controlled robots — is a radio product.
EU: Radio Equipment Directive, with the applicable EN 300 328 (2.4 GHz wideband) or EN 300 220 (sub-GHz) test standards. The CE DoC must reference the RED, not only the Toy Safety Directive. US: FCC Part 15. A transmitter needs an FCC ID issued to the grantee, and the ID must appear on the product. The ID is tied to the grantee company, so a factory cannot simply lend you theirs unless you are buying their existing certified model unchanged. Japan: technical conformity mark (技適) under the Radio Act. Korea: KC certification under the Radio Waves Act, separate from the toy confirmation. The two most common failures are output power above the limit and a frequency band that drifts outside the permitted range. Both are design issues, and both are cheap to fix before tooling and expensive afterwards.
There is also a commercial trap: a supplier may offer a “certified” model and then substitute a different transmitter board to save cost. Specify the exact module and require the module’s certificate number in the PO.
Button cells and Reese’s Law Coin and button cells deserve their own section. A swallowed button cell can cause severe internal injury within hours, and regulators have moved accordingly.
US: Reese’s Law applies to consumer products containing button or coin cells. The battery compartment must require a tool or two independent actions to open, and the product and packaging must carry the prescribed warnings. Toys are in scope. EU: EN 71-1 addresses small parts and battery compartments; the General Product Safety Regulation adds the risk-assessment obligation on top. General rule: for anything a child can hold, the coin cell must not be accessible without a tool. Design implications are concrete: a captive screw, a compartment that cannot be opened by hand, no coin cell in a product for under-threes, and a warning label on the toy and the packaging. If a novelty item has a slide-out battery tray, it fails this test regardless of how well it passes EN 71-3.
Charging: keep the adapter out of the box Charging is where cheap electronics create expensive problems.
A USB-C or micro-USB input is the cleanest option: the toy contains no mains voltage, and the customer uses a charger they already own. Compliance scope stays inside the toy. An included mains adapter turns the shipment into a product with its own safety regime — CE and LVD in the EU, PSE in Japan, KC in Korea, UL/ETL in the US. A cheap unbranded adapter is the single most common reason an otherwise compliant toy fails at customs or gets delisted. A built-in Li-ion pack with a sealed charging port means the toy’s protection circuit is the only thing between the cell and the user. Require over-charge, over-discharge and short-circuit protection, and test it. Our default recommendation for OEM electronics is USB-C charging with no adapter in the carton, and the adapter sold separately where the market needs one. It removes an entire compliance surface for a few cents of BOM.
UN38.3 and shipping lithium batteries Lithium cells are Class 9 dangerous goods. Every lithium battery shipment — including batteries installed in a toy — needs:
UN38.3 test report for the cell or pack MSDS (safety data sheet) UN38.3 test summary Correct declaration and packing, and a state of charge at or below 30% for air transport Installed lithium batteries travel as UN3481 (lithium-ion contained in equipment) or UN3091 (lithium metal contained in equipment). Small packs under the Section II thresholds can often move as cargo with the right documents, but the airline and forwarder decide, not the factory.
In practice, many Yiwu suppliers quote “battery not included” because it removes the dangerous-goods surcharge and the paperwork. That is sometimes the right answer for B2B. It is rarely the right answer for a retail product sold as a gift. Price both versions before you commit.
The inspection checks that matter for electronics Standard AQL II visual inspection does not catch electrical defects. Add these:
Capacity test. Discharge three units and record run time against the spec. Charge cycle. Two full charge/discharge cycles, checking for heating and cut-off at the correct voltage. Drop test. 1 m onto concrete, six faces, three units — check for cracks, battery ejection and loss of function. Motor stall. Hold the wheels or rotor for 5 seconds; the protection should cut in, not melt the housing. Radio range. Test at the claimed range in an open area, not across a warehouse. Sound level. Measure at the distance the standard specifies if the toy has a speaker; volume limits are a real failure point. Battery compartment. Confirm the screw, the tool requirement, and that the compartment cannot be opened by hand. Aging run. 48 hours of continuous operation on a sample to catch overheating and solder failures. Record the results against the serial or batch, not just “pass”. When a container of 3,000 units arrives with a 15% failure rate, the inspection records are what make the factory accept responsibility.
Cost and timeline, roughly Market Reports needed Typical lead time EU EN 71-1/2/3 + EN 62115 + EMC + RED + RoHS + battery regulation docs 4–6 weeks US ASTM F963 + CPSIA + FCC (SDoC or FCC ID) 3–6 weeks Japan ST + PSE (if adapter) + 技適 4–7 weeks Korea KC toy confirmation + KC EMC/radio 4–6 weeks Testing one model family is far cheaper than testing each colourway, so group the range by electronics platform before sending samples. A new PCB or a new transmitter means a new report.
The short version Decide “battery included or not” before quoting — it changes cost, freight and compliance. A radio toy needs four scopes: toy, electrical, EMC and radio, in every market. EN 62115 is the electrical toy standard; EN 71 alone leaves the electrical scope open. Coin cells need a tool-locked compartment and prescribed warnings — this is enforced now. USB-C charging without an adapter removes a whole compliance regime from the carton. UN38.3, MSDS and a test summary are required for every lithium shipment, installed or not. Our RC and electronic toy category shows the platforms we produce and source, and the quality and compliance page lists the reports we coordinate per market, including UN38.3 and FCC. If you are developing an electronic toy, send the electronics architecture — battery type, charging method, radio module — and we will map the test scope and the freight before tooling starts.
The market-by-market document logic is the same one covered in EN71, ASTM F963 and GPSR and Japan ST and Korea KC.

Most of the avoidable cost in this category comes from one decision made too late: whether the battery ships inside the toy. That decision changes the unit cost, the test scope, the freight rate and the returns rate. Make it before you quote, not after.

You send an inquiry for 200 plush toys. Three factories do not reply. The fourth replies with a 1,000-piece minimum and a price 60% above the quote you saw online. You conclude that Chinese factories do not want small business.
They do want it. They just cannot run a production line profitably at 200 pieces, and most do not have a polite way to say so. Understanding the arithmetic changes what you ask for.
Why small orders get ignored A toy factory’s cost per order is mostly fixed:
Fixed cost Approximate Notes Production line setup USD 150–400 Changing fabric, thread, mould Pattern / artwork preparation USD 100–300 Even for a repeat design Material minimum purchase USD 200–800 Fabric and trims sold by the roll/box QC and packing setup USD 80–200 Inspection plan, carton spec Export documentation USD 60–150 Per shipment, regardless of size Fixed total USD 600–1,800 Before a single unit is made At 1,000 pieces that is USD 0.60–1.80 per unit. At 200 pieces it is USD 3.00–9.00 per unit. The factory is not being greedy — a 200-piece order at the 1,000-piece price would be sold at a loss.
This is also why a 200-piece quote often looks absurd. The factory is not padding the price; it is spreading the same fixed cost over one-fifth of the volume.
What is realistic at each volume Volume Realistic outcome Expect to pay 50–99 pcs Stock items only, or sample-level pricing FOB + 50–100% 100–199 pcs Possible with a cooperative factory on a simple design FOB + 30–60% 200–299 pcs Workable for most categories with negotiation FOB + 20–40% 300–499 pcs Normal small-order range, most factories will quote FOB + 10–25% 500+ pcs Standard territory FOB + 0–10% These premiums are not arbitrary. They map roughly to the fixed-cost table above. A factory quoting 200 pieces at only 10% above the 1,000-piece price is either making an error or planning to substitute materials.
Five ways to get to 100–500 pcs 1. Buy stock, not custom (cheapest and fastest)
If your goal is to test whether a product sells, do not customise. Buy an existing stock SKU in small quantity, with your logo on a hang tag or a sticker on the polybag. Many suppliers hold stock at 1 set or 10 pcs. You get a real product in 7 days at near-wholesale pricing, and you learn your sell-through before committing to a mould.
This is the right answer for roughly half of the people who ask us for 200 custom pieces. See stock plush toys as an example of the model.
2. Consolidate with other items (spread the fixed cost)
The fixed cost is per order, not per SKU. If you order 200 pcs of three designs from the same factory, the setup cost is shared across 600 units. Ask explicitly:
Can we combine three SKUs into one production run to reach your minimum?
Many factories will accept 600 total units across three designs where they would refuse 200 of one.
3. Use an agent’s existing order flow (piggyback)
An agent running regular orders with a factory can add your 200 pieces to a production slot that is already being set up. Your marginal cost is materials plus a small handling fee, because the setup is already paid for. This is the single most effective route for genuinely small first orders, and it is a large part of what a sourcing agent actually does.
4. Simplify the design to hit the minimum
A plain round plush with embroidered eyes has a far lower setup cost than a shaped character with printed fabric, appliqué and a 3D nose. If 200 pieces is the constraint, choose the design the factory can run cheaply. Ask: “What is the lowest-MOQ version of this product you can make?” You will often get a different answer than the one in the catalogue.
5. Pay the setup cost separately
Some factories will accept 200 pieces if you pay tooling, plates and pattern-making as a separate one-off charge instead of amortising it. You pay more up front, but you own the pattern and the per-unit price stays honest. Clarify ownership in writing — see sample and tooling ownership.
The inquiry that actually gets a reply Most small-buyer inquiries fail because they ask a question the factory cannot answer cheaply. Compare:
What gets ignored:
Hi, I need 200 plush toys, please send your best price.
What gets a reply:
Subject: 200 pcs + 400 pcs repeat — plush bear, EN71
We are a new brand testing the market. Target: 200 pcs for a test order, with a 400–600 pcs repeat if sell-through is good.
Product: 25 cm plush bear, short-pile fabric, PP cotton, embroidered eyes. Packaging: polybag with printed header card. Testing: EN71-1/-2/-3 reports required.
Please tell us: (1) your MOQ for this exact spec, (2) whether a 200 pcs order is possible at a premium, and (3) the per-unit price at 200, 400 and 1,000 pcs.
Three things make this work: it states the repeat intent, it gives a complete spec so the factory does not have to guess, and it asks for a price ladder so you can see exactly what the small-order premium is. That last point is also a negotiation tool — if 200 pcs costs 40% more than 400 pcs, you may prefer to start at 400.
Three traps in small-batch sourcing Trap 1: accepting a low price with a vague spec. The factory that says “yes, 200 pieces, no problem” and quotes the same price as 1,000 pieces is planning to substitute fabric or filling. Ask for g/m² and filling weight per piece.
Trap 2: shipping 200 pieces by air and calling it sourcing. Air freight on a small order can double the landed cost. For a test order, price the freight before you approve the order. See landed cost.
Trap 3: ordering 200 pieces across five designs. Splitting a small order across many SKUs multiplies the fixed cost five times. Small batch plus wide assortment is the most expensive combination in toy importing.
After the test order Plan the second order before you place the first, because it determines how the factory treats you. Two commitments make a real difference:
Give a target repeat quantity and a date. “If this sells, we will reorder 800 pcs in March” converts you from a nuisance order to a pipeline. Ask what changes at 500 and 1,000 pcs. It tells you the factory’s price ladder and where the step-downs are. Small buyers who communicate a plan get treated as future volume. Small buyers who ask for one cheap order get treated as one cheap order.
When small batch is the wrong answer If your volume is genuinely under 100 pieces and the product must be custom, you are usually better off:
buying a stock item and rebranding the packaging, running a pre-order campaign to prove demand before producing, or choosing a category with lower minimums (fidget and pet toys often start at 1 set or 10 pcs, versus 500 for custom plush). We quote small orders routinely where the category allows it — the MOQ table in llms.txt lists starting quantities per category. If your target is 200 pcs of a custom plush, tell us the spec and the repeat plan, and we will tell you honestly whether the economics work or whether a stock item is the smarter test.
summary:
You send an inquiry for 200 plush toys. Three factories do not reply. The fourth replies with a 1,000-piece minimum and a price 60% above the quote you saw online. You conclude that Chinese factories do not want small business.

They do want it. They just cannot run a production line profitably at 200 pieces, and most do not have a polite way to say so. Understanding the arithmetic changes what you ask for.

A buyer asks for a quote on 1,000 plush toys. The factory says USD 10.00 FOB Ningbo. The buyer budgets USD 10,000. The goods arrive with an actual cost of USD 14,200, and the margin calculation for the whole product line was wrong before the first unit sold.
This is the single most expensive arithmetic error in toy importing, and it happens because FOB is not a cost — it is the price of goods sitting on a ship in China. Everything that happens after that point is also your cost.
Here are the nine items that make up real landed cost, in the order they occur.
The nine cost items # Cost Typical size Who quotes it 1 Goods at FOB baseline Factory 2 Inland freight to port 1–2% Factory / forwarder 3 Export declaration & docs 0.5–1.5% Factory / forwarder 4 Ocean or air freight 8–25% Forwarder 5 Marine insurance 0.3–0.6% Forwarder 6 Destination port charges 2–5% Forwarder / broker 7 Import duty 0–12% of CIF Customs 8 Import VAT / sales tax 0–27% (recoverable) Customs 9 Last mile + FBA inbound 3–12% 3PL / Amazon Add two more that people forget entirely: testing and certification amortised per unit, and a return/damage reserve. Both are real, neither appears on any quote.
A worked example: 1,000 plush toys Assume 1,000 pcs at USD 10.00 FOB Ningbo, LCL shipment to Rotterdam, EU importer.
Item Amount Notes FOB goods USD 10,000 1,000 × 10.00 Inland freight + export docs USD 280 Factory to Ningbo port Ocean freight (LCL) USD 950 ~4.5 CBM at LCL rates Marine insurance USD 45 0.4% of CIF CIF value USD 11,275 Duty is calculated on this Import duty (4.7%) USD 530 EU toy rate, HS 9503 Destination port + clearance USD 420 THC, docs, broker Last mile to warehouse USD 260 Port to 3PL Duty-paid landed cost USD 12,485 Before tax Import VAT (21%, recoverable) USD 2,622 Cash flow, not margin Cash out at clearance USD 15,107 What leaves your account So the landed cost per unit is USD 12.49, not USD 10.00 — a 25% gap. If you are a VAT-registered business, the VAT is reclaimed and your true cost stays at USD 12.49. If you are not registered, or you sell through a marketplace that collects VAT on your behalf, it is a genuine cost or a 60–90 day cash flow hole.
Add certification amortisation. If the EN71 test report cost USD 600 and you order 1,000 pcs, that is USD 0.60 per unit — 6% of the FOB price, invisible on every quote.
Duty rates by market (HS 9503) Market Typical toy duty Notes EU 4.7% On CIF value UK 0% UK Global Tariff USA 0% base Plus additional tariffs on Chinese goods — verify current rate Japan 0% Most toys duty-free Canada 0% Australia 0–5% Depends on subheading Mexico 5–15% Requires NOM compliance The US line deserves emphasis. Between 2018 and 2026 the tariff treatment of Chinese toys changed repeatedly through Section 301 actions and subsequent adjustments. A rate you read in a 2021 blog post may be wrong today by a wide margin. Before you price a US order, check the current HTS 9503 rate plus any active additional duties with your customs broker, not with a website. Getting this wrong on a container is a five-figure error.
VAT is not the same as duty These get conflated constantly:
Duty is a real cost. It never comes back. VAT / sales tax is a pass-through for registered businesses. You pay it at import, reclaim it on your return. It costs you cash flow and administrative effort, not margin. But it matters enormously for pricing decisions if you are:
Not VAT-registered (common for new Amazon sellers) Selling on a marketplace that deems the platform the supplier (Amazon collects and remits, you may not reclaim) Under-capitalised — the VAT on a USD 30,000 shipment is USD 6,300 locked up for weeks The three errors that cost the most 1. Comparing FOB to a competitor’s DDP price. A DDP quote includes freight, duty and delivery. Comparing it to a bare FOB number makes the DDP supplier look 40% more expensive when they may be cheaper all-in. Always normalise both to landed cost per unit.
2. Forgetting the carton dimensions. LCL and air freight price on volume, not weight, for toys. A plush toy carton that is 20% larger because the factory over-packaged costs you 20% more in freight. Ask for carton dimensions before confirming the order, and challenge them if the fill ratio is poor. See packaging cost comparison for how carton design affects both packaging and freight.
3. Assuming the first shipment’s freight rate is the normal rate. Freight rates on China–Europe and China–US lanes have moved 2–3x within single quarters in recent years. A quote valid for 30 days is normal; a quote you assume holds for a year is not. Build a freight contingency into your unit economics, typically 15–20% above the current quote.
A simple template you can reuse FOB unit price = A Units per carton = B Cartons = C = total_units / B CBM total = D Freight per CBM = E Freight total = F = D * E Insurance = G = (A*total + F) * 0.004 CIF value = H = A*total + F + G Duty = I = H * duty_rate Port + clearance = J Last mile / FBA inbound = K Testing amortised = L = test_cost / total_units Landed cost total = H + I + J + K + L Landed cost per unit = above / total_units Landed multiple = landed per unit / FOB unit price Track the landed multiple. For sea freight from China to the EU or US, a healthy range is 1.25–1.45x on FOB for mid-value toys. Above 1.6x usually means you are shipping inefficiently — too much air, poor carton fill, or a small order paying LCL minimums. Below 1.2x usually means something is missing from the calculation.
Where this changes your sourcing decision Once you calculate landed cost properly, three things become visible that were invisible at FOB:
A factory 5% cheaper on FOB but 15% bulkier in cartons is more expensive landed. Freight eats the saving. A small order’s LCL minimum makes unit economics brutal. 300 pcs by LCL can carry the same freight cost as 1,000 pcs, tripling the per-unit freight. This is why MOQ decisions are really freight decisions. DDP is often the right answer for first orders, not because it is cheap, but because it removes four cost lines you would otherwise have to estimate badly. Our shipping and logistics page lists transit times and Incoterms by lane, and we quote landed cost per unit — not just FOB — when you share carton data and the destination warehouse.
A practical next step Take your last three quotes and put them through the template above. If your landed multiple is above 1.5x, the problem is usually carton volume or shipping mode, not the factory price. If you cannot fill in lines 2, 3, 6 and 9, that is exactly the information a sourcing agent should be supplying before you place a deposit.
Ask your supplier for these five numbers with any quote — they cost nothing to provide and make every comparison honest:
FOB unit price and MOQ Carton dimensions, carton weight, units per carton HS code they declare Test reports on file and their cost Lead time from deposit to carton-ready

A buyer asks for a quote on 1,000 plush toys. The factory says USD 10.00 FOB Ningbo. The buyer budgets USD 10,000. The goods arrive with an actual cost of USD 14,200, and the margin calculation for the whole product line was wrong before the first unit sold.

This is the single most expensive arithmetic error in toy importing, and it happens because FOB is not a cost — it is the price of goods sitting on a ship in China. Everything that happens after that point is also your cost.

Most buyers assume pet toys are regulated like children’s toys. They are not — and that misunderstanding cuts both ways. It makes some buyers spend money on certificates nobody asks for, and it lets others ship products that get stopped at the border or pulled from Amazon.
Here is the accurate picture for pet toys entering the United States.
The key distinction: pet toys are not children’s products The Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act (CPSIA) applies to products designed or intended primarily for children 12 and under. A dog chew toy is not a children’s product. That means:
No Children’s Product Certificate (CPC) is required No third-party CPSIA testing is mandated CPSIA phthalate and lead limits do not legally apply This is a genuine difference from a plush toy sold to a three-year-old. If a supplier tells you a pet toy “needs a CPC”, they are either misunderstanding the rule or reusing a children’s-toy template.
The exception that catches people: a product marketed to children and pets — a plush animal sold as a children’s toy that a dog also plays with — is a children’s product and CPSIA applies in full. Marketing copy determines classification. Do not describe a pet product as suitable for toddlers.
What does apply 1. FDA rules for edible chews and treats
If the product is intended to be eaten — rawhide, dental chews with digestible content, treats, anything with a nutritional claim — it falls under FDA animal food regulation, not toy regulation. That brings facility registration, prior notice for imports, and labeling requirements. A rubber chew toy does not. A chew with a treat pocket where the treat is sold separately usually does not either, but the labeling must be clear that the toy is not food.
2. State chemical laws
California Proposition 65 is the one that actually triggers claims. It requires a warning for exposure to listed chemicals above threshold. For pet products the practical exposure is:
Phthalates in soft PVC or TPR Lead in painted or coated parts Diisocyanates in polyurethane foam A Prop 65 warning label is not a defect — it is a disclosure. Many large retailers simply refuse products that require one, which is the real commercial constraint. Ask for a phthalate-free and lead-free formulation and get test data, rather than accepting a warning label and losing the account.
Several other states (Washington, Maine, Vermont, New York) have their own chemical reporting rules that increasingly cover pet products. If your channel is a large US retailer, they will ask.
3. Flammability, if the product contains fabric or foam
There is no federal pet-toy flammability standard. But if you sell a plush or foam pet bed or a stuffed pet toy through a retailer with its own standards policy, they may apply ASTM F963 or California TB 117 testing by contract, even though the law does not require it. Read the retailer’s vendor requirements, not just the law.
4. Amazon and other marketplace requirements
This is where most sellers actually get blocked. Amazon requires, for pet supplies:
Product safety documentation on request, typically a test report from an ISO 17025-accredited lab Country of origin labeling Allergen and material disclosure in some categories Amazon does not publish a fixed list of required tests for pet toys, and requirements change. Practical approach: get a test report covering heavy metals, phthalates and azo dyes from an accredited lab before you list. It costs a few hundred dollars per SKU and clears most requests.
Labeling that is actually required Federal law does not mandate a specific pet-toy label. What you should still put on retail packaging:
Country of origin (“Made in China”) — required for imported goods under US Customs rules Manufacturer or importer name and address — required for most consumer goods Material content, especially for chew-resistant claims “Not a children’s toy” if there is any chance of the product being used by a child Warnings: “Remove toy if damaged”, “Not for aggressive chewers”, “Supervise use” The “not for aggressive chewers” line is commercially important. Most pet-toy returns are from a dog destroying a product in ten minutes, and a clear chew-strength claim reduces damage claims.
Chew strength is the real quality spec For pet toys, the specification that matters more than any certificate is chew strength, and it is the one Chinese factories most often leave vague. Define it:
Level Typical use Material Soft / plush Gentle chewers, puppies, fetch Plush with minimal filling, no squeaker Medium Average adult dogs TPR, natural rubber, layered fabric Tough Strong chewers Dense natural rubber, nylon core Power chewer Aggressive destroyers Solid nylon, hard rubber, no fabric Test it by sending samples to real dogs, or ask the factory for a tensile and tear test report. Our pet toy range is specified by chew level rather than by “durable” as a claim.
What to ask your supplier for 1. Material composition, by part, with % content 2. Phthalate and heavy-metal test report, accredited lab, current batch 3. Country of origin marking on product and carton 4. Chew strength rating and the test method used 5. Whether any part is edible, and if so, FDA compliance documentation 6. Retail packaging artwork approval before print That list is short, and on a first order it separates suppliers who understand the US market from those who are reselling a domestic product spec.
Summary Pet toys are not CPSIA children’s products; no CPC is required Edible chews move into FDA animal food territory Prop 65 and state chemical laws are the real claim risk Amazon will ask for accredited-lab reports; get them before listing Chew strength is the specification that decides return rates For the more general compliance picture across toy categories, see toy safety certifications and our quality and compliance process.
